paragraphs: Here's the big idea, friend: God's people don't have to fake it with Him. They sat by the rivers of Babylon and wept (Psalm 137:1), and the psalm doesn't scold them for it. When their captors wanted songs of joy, they hung up their harps and asked, "How can we sing a song of the LORD in a foreign land?" (Psalm 137:3-4). Some days the honest thing is to sit down and cry, and this psalm is in the Bible to say that's allowed.

Now look at what else the writer does with all that hurt. The writer doesn't swallow it. The writer promises to remember Jerusalem, and then brings the pain to the LORD: "Remember, O LORD, the sons of Edom on the day Jerusalem fell" (Psalm 137:7). That's a person handing the heaviest thing they own to God instead of carrying it alone. I think that's the part to hold onto, baker.

And then comes the last line, and I'm not going to dress it up. "Blessed is he who seizes your infants and dashes them against the rocks" (Psalm 137:9). It's raw, it's heavy, and the psalm ends without tidying it. I think the lesson is that God lets His people say the real thing out loud to Him, and so next time you're hurting, you can bring Him the whole thing too.
